title: Cervical cancer: HPV oncogenesis, Bethesda screening, FIGO 2018 staging, radical surgery and chemoradiation
subject: ss-obg
refs: Gynecology by Ten Teachers 21e Ch 16 (Premalignant and malignant disease of the cervix)
FIGO Cancer Report: Cancer of the cervix uteri (2021 update)

steps.say: High-risk human papillomavirus persistent infection represents the essential causative agent in over ninety-five percent of cervical carcinomas. Oncoproteins E6 and E7 drive neoplastic cellular transformation: E6 binds and degrades the p53 tumor suppressor via ubiquitin ligase, while E7 dissociates the retinoblastoma protein.
steps.tx: Persistent infection with **high-risk HPV** (predominantly genotypes 16 and 18) drives cervical oncogenesis. Viral **E6 oncoprotein** binds and degrades the **p53 tumor suppressor** protein via ubiquitin ligase, while viral **E7 oncoprotein** inactivates the **retinoblastoma protein** (pRb), releasing E2F to promote uncontrolled cellular proliferation.

steps.say: Cytological cervical screening is reported internationally using the standardized Bethesda System. Epithelial cell abnormalities are categorized into atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion representing transient HPV or CIN 1, and high-grade SIL representing true premalignancy.
steps.tx: The **Bethesda System** categorizes cervical cytology into **ASC-US**, ASC-H, **LSIL** (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, correlating with transient HPV infection and CIN 1), and **HSIL** (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, representing true premalignant CIN 2/3 and carcinoma in situ), directing triage to colposcopy.

rows: Reactive changes or early HPV atypia
Reflex HPV testing: colposcopy if high-risk HPV positive
Direct colposcopic evaluation mandatory for all patients
Colposcopy (or repeat cytology at 12 months if young)
Immediate colposcopy or immediate diagnostic loop excision (LLETZ)

steps.say: The updated FIGO 2018 staging system formally incorporates modern cross-sectional imaging and pathological assessment into clinical staging. Under this revised framework, pelvic nodal metastasis upgrades disease to Stage IIIC1, while para-aortic lymph node metastasis designates Stage IIIC2.
steps.tx: The **FIGO 2018 staging** system permits cross-sectional imaging (MRI, PET-CT) and surgical pathology to allocate stage. Lymph node involvement is explicitly staged as **Stage IIIC**, subdividing into **Stage IIIC1** for pelvic lymph node metastasis and **Stage IIIC2** for para-aortic nodal metastasis.

nodes.label: Document invasive cervical carcinoma on histological biopsy
Perform pelvic MRI and whole-body FDG PET-CT for anatomical and nodal staging
Identify positive pelvic lymph nodes: assign Stage IIIC1
Identify positive para-aortic lymph nodes: assign Stage IIIC2

steps.say: Microinvasive cervical carcinoma with minimal stromal penetration carries a negligible risk of lymph node metastasis. Stage IA1 disease, defined by measured stromal invasion depth of three millimeters or less without lymphovascular space invasion, is treated conservatively by cold-knife cervical conization.
steps.tx: **Stage IA1** microinvasive carcinoma, defined by stromal invasion depth <= 3 mm and horizontal spread <= 7 mm without lymphovascular invasion, carries a nodal metastasis risk < 1 percent. It is safely treated with **cervical conization** with negative surgical margins, preserving reproductive function.

left.title: Stage IA1 Microinvasive Carcinoma
points: Stromal invasion depth <= 3 mm, no LVSI
Conservative therapeutic conization with clear margins curative

right.title: Stage IA2 Microinvasive Carcinoma
points: Stromal invasion depth > 3 mm and <= 5 mm
Nodal metastasis risk rises to 3 to 5%
Requires modified radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy

steps.say: Early-stage invasive cervical cancer without parametrial involvement is managed definitively with radical surgery. Type C radical hysterectomy, historically known as the Wertheim-Meigs operation, removes the uterus, parametria, upper third of the vagina, and regional pelvic lymph nodes.
steps.tx: Early invasive disease (Stage IB1, IB2, IIA1) is treated with Type C **radical hysterectomy** (Wertheim-Meigs procedure) and bilateral **pelvic lymphadenectomy**. This entails wide resection of parametrial tissue, paracolpos, upper third of the vagina, and systematic removal of external iliac, internal iliac, and obturator nodes.

rows: Removal of cervix and uterus only
Resection of medial half of parametria
Stage IA1 with LVSI or Stage IA2
Full unroofing of ureter to bladder
Lateral to iliac vessels with fascial strip

steps.say: The landmark international LACC clinical trial radically transformed the surgical management of early cervical cancer. The prospective trial demonstrated that open abdominal radical hysterectomy achieves superior disease-free and overall survival compared to minimally invasive laparoscopic or robotic-assisted surgery.
steps.tx: The landmark **LACC trial** demonstrated that **open radical hysterectomy** yields significantly higher disease-free and **overall survival** compared to minimally invasive laparoscopic or robotic techniques (which carry a 4-fold higher local recurrence risk), establishing open laparotomy as the surgical gold standard.

left.title: Open Abdominal Approach (LACC Gold Standard)
points: Lower rate of pelvic peritoneal recurrence
Eliminates tumor spillage from uterine manipulators and pneumoperitoneum

right.title: Minimally Invasive Surgery (Laparoscopic/Robotic)
points: Statistically significant increase in mortality (hazard ratio 6.0)
Restricted or contraindicated for routine radical hysterectomy

steps.say: Locally advanced cervical cancer invading parametrial tissues or extending down the vagina is definitively treated with non-surgical oncological therapy. Standard definitive therapy combines concurrent chemoradiation with weekly intravenous cisplatin, external beam pelvic radiation, and high-dose-rate intracavitary brachytherapy.
steps.tx: Locally advanced cervical carcinoma (Stage IB3, IIA2, IIB, III, IVA) is treated with definitive **concurrent chemoradiation**. This combines weekly **cisplatin** (40 mg/m2) with external beam radiotherapy and image-guided **intracavitary brachytherapy**, achieving excellent locoregional pelvic disease control and long-term overall survival without operative morbidity.

nodes.label: Identify locally advanced stage (parametrial involvement or tumor > 4 cm)
External beam radiotherapy (45 to 50 Gy) directed to pelvis and nodal basins
Administer concurrent weekly intravenous cisplatin (40 mg/m2)
Deliver image-guided high-dose-rate (HDR) intracavitary brachytherapy boost

steps.say: Young women with early-stage invasive cervical cancer who strongly desire future childbearing can be offered conservative fertility-sparing surgery. Radical abdominal or vaginal trachelectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy is indicated for Stage IA2 and IB1 tumors measuring two centimeters or less.
steps.tx: In young patients desiring fertility, **radical trachelectomy** (Dargent procedure or abdominal approach) with pelvic lymphadenectomy is an established option for Stage IA2 to IB1 tumors measuring <= 2 cm without deep stromal invasion, achieving excellent oncological control and viable pregnancy rates.
